units.translation: But wrongly ὀἃ [the relative pronoun] in M at the end of lines 570 and 578, which I used in such a way that at v. 572 and 581, where the simple ὀἃ is read in M, I doubled it, 572 οὐράνι᾽ ἄχη, ὀὰ ὀâ [heavenly griefs, alas alas], and in the antistrophe 581 δαιμόνι᾽ ἄχη, ba ba [divine griefs, alas alas], since it is not likely that the poet preferred a full iambic tripody to a dimeter, about which I spoke in Philologus vol. 13 p. 479.

However, it is not said only of lions, but also of the cubs of other wild animals, such as wolves, which Eustathius p. 1395, 47 and 1625, 47 and Aelian N.A. 7, 47 noted: τῶν δὲ ὑστρίχων καὶ τῶν τοιούτων ἀγρίων τὰ ἔκγονα ὄβρια ( καὶ ὀβρίκαλα [and obrikala] Nauck adds) καλεῖται [the offspring of porcupines and such wild animals are called obria (and obrikala)], and Euripides in the Peliades mentions the name, and Aeschylus in the Agamemnon and in the Dictyulci (fr. 43).
Rightly therefore Hesychius explains ὀβρικάλοις [to the cubs] generally as τοῖς τῶν θηρίων ἐκγόνοις [the offspring of wild animals].
and of fierce lions and of all wild beasts that love the breast, to their cubs.
obria and obrikala: the cubs of lions and wolves. Aeschylus in Dictyulci.

Here too in the copies (for this part of the play is lost from M) it is ὄμβριμον [strong].

Of impetuous warriors Sept. 794 πέπτωκεν ἀνδρῶν ὀβρίμων κομπάσματα [the boasts of mighty men have fallen] (where in some copies ὀμβρίμων [mighty], a frequent error in manuscripts, on which see Thes. vol. 6 p. 1718).
μίσος ὄβριμον ἀστοῖς [mighty hatred for the citizens], i.e. heavy.
Onca, epithet of Minerva among the Phoenicians

Strangely the scholium on v. 164 says: Ογκαία Ἀθηνᾶ τιμᾶται παρὰ Θηβαίοις, Ὄγκα δὲ παρὰ τοῖς Φοίνιξι [Oncaian Athena is honored among the Thebans, but Onca among the Phoenicians]. For Minerva is nowhere called OὈγκαία [Oncaian], but Ογκα [Onca], and Ὀγκαῖαι πύλαι [Oncaian gates] is the name of the Theban gates, which were also called Ωγύγιαι πύλαι [Ogygian gates]: on which see Unger in Theb. Parad. vol. 1 p. 267. Rightly therefore in the scholium a later hand has: Ὄγκα παρὰ Φοίνιξιν ἡ Ἀθηνᾶ. καὶ ὁ Κάδμος γάρ [Onca among the Phoenicians is Athena. And Cadmus indeed] (the founder of Thebes) was a Phoenician.

πύλας – τὰς τῆς Ἀθηνᾶς τῆς Ὀγκαίας, ἀφ᾿ ἧς καὶ αἱ πύλαι Ογκαῖαι [the gates – those of Athena Oncaia, from whom also the gates are called Oncaian], again wrongly Ογκαίας [Oncaian] is said instead of ῎Ογκας [Onca], but rightly at the end of the scholium: Κάδμος τῇ Αἰγυπτίᾳ [Cadmus in the Egyptian] (wrongly he names Egyptian instead of Phoenician) φωνή ταύτην (Ἀθηνᾶν) ἐτίμησεν ἐκεῖ ῎Ογκαν [in the language honored her (Athena) there as Onca].
